# A first open water mile: a 10-week plan (active start)

*Generated by the Don't Die Retired guidance engine on 21 November 2026 from 44 sourced statements. Draft for review: not yet checked by a coach, physiotherapist or doctor.*

## The challenge

About 1.6 km (1 mile) of continuous swimming outdoors, with no lane ropes or walls to rest on, often in cold water. [1, 2, 3, 4]

**Before this plan:** If you cannot yet swim 400 metres without stopping, build up to it in the pool, or take lessons, before you start this plan. [5, 6, 7]

## Before you start

- If you have a health condition or are worried about your health, speak to your GP (family doctor) before you start training. [6, 8]
- Start from your current level and build up gradually; repeating a week is fine and is part of the plan, not a failure. [5, 6, 7]

## How the plan works

- Do most of your training at an easy, conversational effort, about 2 to 3 out of 10, where you could hold a full conversation. Keep a small share for harder work. [9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14]
- Increase your training a little at a time. Big week-to-week jumps (more than about 30 per cent) were linked with more overuse injuries in a study of 874 new runners; the familiar 10 per cent rule is a sensible cap but is not firmly proven. [6, 15, 16]
- Every third or fourth week, ease back on volume to let your body absorb the work before building again; older runners and people under other stress may do best with every third week. [11, 17, 18, 19]
- Build one long session a week at an easy effort, growing towards the length and duration of the challenge itself. [2, 11, 20, 21]
- Know the real demands of your challenge (distance, total climb, time on your feet, altitude) and make sure your plan builds towards them. [1, 2, 3, 4]
- Plan rest days into every week, and take an easier day when your legs are heavy. [6, 11, 13, 22, 23]
- Do strength exercises for the whole body on at least two days a week. In trials, strength training cut sports injuries to about a third. [2, 5, 7, 24, 25, 26]
- In the final two weeks, cut your training volume by roughly 40 to 60 per cent while keeping the same number of sessions and some of the same effort, so you arrive fresh. [11, 20, 27, 28, 29]
- Use the pool to practise what open water needs and a pool does not teach you, looking up to sight every five to ten strokes and breathing to both sides, and learn to tread water so you can rest. [30, 31]
- Practise floating on your back at a supervised pool or venue so you can do it without thinking. Tilt your head back with your ears under the water, spread your arms and legs, and keep your breathing calm; your legs may sink, and that is fine. If cold water takes your breath away, float for about a minute until your breathing is under control, then call for help or swim to safety. [32, 33]

## Week by week

Rest on Mondays and Fridays. Strength and balance (about 30 minutes, routine below) on Wednesdays and Sundays. Why each part is there, and what changes each week, follows the table. The Saturday continuous swim is the key session: at a steady pace you could keep up all day, in the pool at first and later at a supervised open water venue with others.

| Week | Tue | Thu | Sat: continuous swim | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | easy swim, 30 min | easy swim, 30 min | 800 metres |  |
| 2 | easy swim, 30 min | sighting and breathing drills | 900 metres |  |
| 3 | easy swim, 30 min | sighting and breathing drills | 750 metres | easier week |
| 4 | easy swim, 30 min | sighting and breathing drills | 1,050 metres |  |
| 5 | easy swim, 30 min | sighting and breathing drills | 1,200 metres |  |
| 6 | easy swim, 30 min | sighting and breathing drills | 950 metres | easier week |
| 7 | easy swim, 30 min | sighting and breathing drills | 1,400 metres |  |
| 8 | easy swim, 30 min | sighting and breathing drills | 1,600 metres |  |
| 9 | easy swim, 30 min | easy swim, 30 min | 950 metres | taper begins: same sessions, less of each |
| 10 | easy swim, 20 min | rest | **the challenge** | event week: rest, sleep, eat well |

*Sighting and breathing drills*: in the pool, lift your eyes to sight every five to ten strokes and breathe to both sides, and practise treading water. 

## What each part of the plan is for

- **The Saturday continuous swim.** The long session prepares you for the length of the day itself. Its pace does not matter; covering the time or distance does, so keep it at a conversational effort. [1, 2, 11]
- **The easy swims.** Easy sessions add fitness without leaving you too tired for the long session. Top endurance athletes do about four in five of their sessions at this low effort. [9, 10]
- **Sighting and breathing drills.** Sighting and breathing to both sides are what open water asks of you that a pool does not, and practising them in the pool makes them a habit before you need them. [30]
- **Strength and balance.** Strength and balance work is what keeps you in one piece. In trials it cut sports injuries to about a third, and it is part of the official guidance for everyone on at least two days a week. [5, 24]
- **Rest days.** Rest days are when your body recovers from the work and adapts to it. The NHS's beginner running plan puts a rest day between every run. [6, 17]
- **Easier weeks.** An easier week, every third week in this plan, lets the tiredness of the previous weeks clear, so your fitness can rebound before you build again. [11, 17, 19]
- **The taper.** Cutting back in the final weeks lets your muscles recover and your body refuel, so you arrive fresh rather than tired. In research, a two-week taper improved performance. [27, 28]

## Each week, and why

**Week 1: setting the pattern.**

- Five sessions and two rest days. The continuous swim starts at 800 metres.
- Why the long session: it gets you used to the hours you will spend out on the day; pace does not matter [1, 2, 11]
- Tuesday's easy swim: it adds fitness while leaving you fresh for the long session [9, 10]
- Strength and balance, Wednesday and Sunday: it protects you from injury (about a third of the injuries in trials) [5, 24]
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [6, 17]

**Week 2: building.**

- The continuous swim grows to 900 metres, up from 800 metres in your last full week.
- Why only this much more: big jumps from one week to the next are linked with overuse injuries. [6, 15, 16]
- New this week, sighting and breathing drills on Thursday: it turns sighting and two-sided breathing into habits before you need them outdoors [30]
- Strength and balance, Wednesday and Sunday: it protects you from injury (about a third of the injuries in trials) [5, 24]

**Week 3: an easier week.**

- The continuous swim eases back to 750 metres.
- Why ease off: it lets the last two weeks' tiredness clear so your fitness can catch up [11, 17, 19]
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [6, 17]

**Week 4: building.**

- The continuous swim grows to 1,050 metres, up from 900 metres in your last full week.
- Why the long session: it gets you used to the hours you will spend out on the day; pace does not matter [1, 2, 11]
- Sighting and breathing drills again on Thursday: it turns sighting and two-sided breathing into habits before you need them outdoors [30]
- Tuesday's easy swim: it adds fitness while leaving you fresh for the long session [9, 10]

**Week 5: building.**

- The continuous swim grows to 1,200 metres, up from 1,050 metres in your last full week.
- Why only this much more: big jumps from one week to the next are linked with overuse injuries. [6, 15, 16]
- Strength and balance, Wednesday and Sunday: it protects you from injury (about a third of the injuries in trials) [5, 24]

**Week 6: an easier week.**

- The continuous swim eases back to 950 metres.
- Why ease off: it lets the last two weeks' tiredness clear so your fitness can catch up [11, 17, 19]
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [6, 17]

**Week 7: building.**

- The continuous swim grows to 1,400 metres, up from 1,200 metres in your last full week.
- Why the long session: it gets you used to the hours you will spend out on the day; pace does not matter [1, 2, 11]
- Tuesday's easy swim: it adds fitness while leaving you fresh for the long session [9, 10]

**Week 8: your biggest week.**

- Your longest continuous swim of the plan, 1,600 metres, as close to the real day as training gets.
- Why the long session: it gets you used to the hours you will spend out on the day; pace does not matter [1, 2, 11]
- Sighting and breathing drills again on Thursday: it turns sighting and two-sided breathing into habits before you need them outdoors [30]
- Strength and balance, Wednesday and Sunday: it protects you from injury (about a third of the injuries in trials) [5, 24]

**Week 9: taper.**

- The continuous swim drops to 950 metres, but you keep every session.
- Why less now: your muscles recover and your body refuels, so you arrive fresh [27, 28]
- Tuesday's easy swim: it adds fitness while leaving you fresh for the long session [9, 10]
- Keep both strength sessions but make them lighter: same sessions, less of each.
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [6, 17]

**Week 10: the challenge.**

- One short, easy outing early in the week and plenty of rest: your muscles recover and your body refuels, so you arrive fresh [27, 28]
- No strength sessions this week; arrive rested.


## Looking after your body

- Include balance work; for older adults the official guidance pairs it with strength on two days a week, the NHS says balance and flexibility work twice a week can reduce the risk of falling, and balance (proprioception) training also reduced injuries in trials. [5, 7, 24, 25, 26]
- Stretch after a long day if it feels good, but do not rely on stretching to prevent injury; trials found it made no difference, unlike strength and balance work. [2, 24]
- Weight-bearing activity such as walking and running helps keep bones strong. [5]
- If you have osteoporosis or a high risk of fractures, ask your GP (family doctor) whether high-impact exercise is right for you before adding it. [25]
- Exercise that challenges your balance and builds functional strength, progressed regularly and kept up over time, helps prevent falls as you get older; tai chi is another option. A review of 108 trials found exercise cut the rate of falls by about a quarter, and balance and functional exercises combined with strength work probably cut it by about a third. [34, 35, 36, 37]
- Keep a regular sleep routine through training, going to bed and getting up at around the same time each day; good sleep is part of recovery, and on multi-day trips a warm enough sleeping bag and mat matter more than people expect. [22, 28, 38]
- If you miss a session, do not worry about it; carry on with the plan, or repeat a week if you need to. [6, 28]

**Strength and balance routine (twice a week).** Squats, lunges, a core exercise such as a plank, and a balance exercise such as standing on one leg. Start with your own body weight, two sets of 8 to 12 slow repetitions, and add load only when that feels easy. [2, 5, 7, 24, 25, 26]

## Fuel, drink and feet

- On long days eat regularly on the move, a little and often from a variety of foods, rather than one big meal before you start. [2, 39, 40]
- Use your long sessions to practise exactly what you will eat and drink on the day, building up gradually so your stomach gets used to it. Nothing new on the day. [28, 39, 41]

## On the day

- Start slower than you think you need to; early miles feel easy and are where most people overdo it. [3, 4, 9, 28, 41, 42]
- Wear a brightly coloured swim cap and tow a float, so boats and other water users can see you and you have something to hold if you tire. [30, 43, 44, 45, 46]
- Before you get in, check the forecast, tides, currents and the water itself, and plan where you will get in and out, with a second exit in case. [30, 43, 44, 46]
- If you will wear a wetsuit on the day, train in that same wetsuit beforehand rather than changing kit for the event. [47]
- Your body temperature can keep falling for a while after you get out of cold water (afterdrop), so dry off and get into warm, windproof clothes and a hat as soon as you are out, and move about to make heat. After a short swim a warm shower is enough; avoid very hot water, and do not hold a hot water bottle against numb skin, which burns easily. [48, 49, 50]

## Safety

- If you have osteoporosis or a high risk of fractures, ask your GP (family doctor) whether high-impact exercise is right for you before adding it. [25]
- Drink when you are thirsty rather than to a schedule. Drinking far more than you need can dilute the body's sodium, which can be dangerous; it affects walkers and recreational exercisers as well as racers. [51]
- Call 999 (911 in the US) for tight or squeezing chest pain, pain spreading to the arms, neck or jaw, severe breathlessness, or if someone collapses. Do not drive yourself to hospital. [52]
- Stop if something does not feel right, and get it checked rather than training through it. [6, 28]
- Never swim alone in open water. Swim with a friend, a club or at a supervised venue, and tell someone on land where you are going and when you will be back. [30, 33, 43, 44, 53, 54, 55]
- In water of 15°C (59°F) or below, cold water shock makes you gasp and breathe fast. Walk in slowly rather than jumping or diving, and give your breathing 60 to 90 seconds to settle before you swim. If you get into difficulty, lean back and float until it passes. [32, 33, 43, 44, 48]
- Get out if your stroke slows, weakens or loses its rhythm, or if you are shivering or slurring your words; these are signs that you are getting too cold. [30, 44, 56]
- If you or someone else is in trouble in the water, call 999 or 112 and ask for the Coastguard (911 in the US). Do not go in after them; tell them to float and throw them something that floats. [43, 44]
- In the sea, choose a lifeguarded beach and swim between the red and yellow flags. If a rip current carries you out, do not swim against it. If you can stand, wade; if not, float. Then swim or wade parallel to the shore until you are out of the rip before heading in, and raise your hand and shout for help. [57, 58, 59]
